origin_region: Tamil Nadu · Nilgiri Hills (high estates around Ooty and Kotagiri)
cultivar: Chinary and hybrid seedling bushes plus UPASI clones
processing: Orthodox black tea from leaf plucked on cold, clear winter mornings after frost; a long, cool wither, gentle rolling, careful oxidation and light firing preserve an unusually floral aroma. Some estates stop oxidation early for an oolong-like version.
harvest_season: The brief cold season, roughly December to early February, when night temperatures on the high estates drop close to freezing.
appearance_dry: Tightly twisted dark leaf with some golden-tipped strands.
appearance_wet: Coppery-olive leaf with a fresh, floral smell.
taste_profile: Markedly floral and fruity — honeysuckle, citrus peel, sometimes a hint of mint — on a light, sweet body with soft tannin.

brewing.notes: A touch cooler than ordinary Nilgiri and no milk; it re-steeps well.

vintage_note: Sold as a seasonal special with the winter and the year on the label ('Winter Frost 2025', 'Frost Tea Jan 2026') from estates such as Glendale, Havukal, Chamraj and Thiashola, reaching importers from about January in limited quantity. Buy it in the first half of the year and drink within twelve months; it is not an ageing tea.
description:
Nilgiri frost tea is a winter speciality from the highest estates in the Nilgiri Hills, made from leaf plucked on cold, clear mornings between roughly December and early February, when night temperatures drop close to freezing. The cold slows the bushes, concentrates the shoots and produces a black tea far more aromatic than anything the same gardens make in the warm months.

Factories handle the frost leaf with more care than the everyday crop: a long, cool wither, gentle orthodox rolling, controlled oxidation and a light firing. Some estates stop oxidation early for an oolong-like 'frost' tea, but most sell it as a fully oxidised black.

The cup is bright gold to light orange and unmistakably floral and fruity: honeysuckle, citrus peel, sometimes a hint of mint, on a light, sweet body with soft tannin. Brew it a touch cooler than ordinary Nilgiri, around 90 °C, for three minutes, and try a second and third steep; milk would waste it.

It is sold as a seasonal special with the winter and the year on the label from estates such as Glendale, Havukal, Chamraj and Thiashola, and it shows up with importers from about January in limited quantity. Buy it in the first half of the year and drink it within twelve months; it is not an ageing tea.

If you have only met Nilgiri in tea bags, a frost lot is the best argument for the region.
